Vial
vī´al
n. (a shallow bowl; rendering Greek phiale)
From Greek phiale, a broad flat bowl used for pouring libations. The modern picture of a narrow glass tube is wrong; a vial in Scripture is a wide dish that empties at once.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

A vial is a shallow bowl. Revelation gives them two contents. The first is prayer: the four beasts and elders fall before the Lamb, “having every one of them harps, and golden vials full of odours, which are the prayers of saints” (Rev 5:8). The second is wrath: “Go your ways, and pour out the vials of the wrath of God upon the earth” (Rev 16:1). The same vessel-shape holds both, and the shape matters — a broad bowl is not poured gradually but tipped and emptied.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a vial as a phial, a small bottle of thin glass, used particularly by apothecaries and druggists.

expand to see more

VIAL, n. A phial; a small bottle of thin glass, used particularly by apothecaries and druggists.

VIAL, v.t. To put in a vial.

Key Scripture

Rev 5:8 — "And when he had taken the book, the four beasts and four and twenty elders fell down before the Lamb, having every one of them harps, and golden vials full of odours, which are the prayers of saints."

Rev 16:1 — "And I heard a great voice out of the temple saying to the seven angels, Go your ways, and pour out the vials of the wrath of God upon the earth."

Rev 8:4 — "And the smoke of the incense, which came with the prayers of the saints, ascended up before God out of the angel's hand."

Psa 141:2 — "Let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense; and the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice."

Modern Corruption

Prayer is imagined as vanishing on utterance, when Revelation shows it collected and kept in bowls — and judgment is imagined as arbitrary, when it too is stored before it is poured.

expand to see more

Revelation 5:8 answers a question every discouraged believer asks: where do the prayers go? They are collected. Golden vials full of odours, which are the prayers of saints, are held in heaven before the throne, and Revelation 8:4 shows the smoke of the incense with the prayers ascending up before God out of the angel's hand. Nothing prayed in faith has evaporated. It is in a bowl, kept, and it is not empty.

The parallel with the vials of wrath is deliberate and sobering. Both are stored, both are full, and both are eventually poured out completely rather than dispensed by degrees. Judgment delayed is not judgment cancelled; it is judgment accumulating in a bowl. That is the same doctrine Paul states as treasuring up wrath against the day of wrath (Rom 2:5), and it should make a patient God look more serious rather than less.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek phiale (G5357), a broad shallow bowl for libations — the only New Testament vessel that holds both saints' prayers and God's wrath.

expand to see more

Greek phiale (G5357) — bowl, vial; Revelation 5:8, 15:7, 16:1-17.

Greek thumiama (G2368) — incense, odours; Revelation 5:8, identified as the prayers of saints.

Hebrew qetoreth (H7004) — incense; Psalm 141:2, let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense.

Usage

"“Golden vials full of odours, which are the prayers of saints” — prayer collected and kept."

"“Pour out the vials of the wrath of God” — the same shape, tipped and emptied."

"“Let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense” — the psalm behind the image."
